method: Same-agent bilingual close reading, reverse paraphrase of each explanatory paragraph, and exact formula/macro/token/identifier comparison. No independent human or native-speaker review is claimed.
scope: Undecidability introduction: physical-function example, effective decision, cardinality, Halting Problem, and first-order validity decision problem.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: Counting radioactive decays in successive one-second intervals looks impossible to compute, but inability to imagine a method is not a proof. If the universe ends after finitely many seconds, the function has a finite domain and a sufficiently large table or Turing transition diagram computes it abstractly.
samples.checks: The nth-interval definition, finite-time hypothesis, distant-future contraction example, and finite-domain conclusion are retained without treating the physical speculation as established fact.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: A yes/no question is effectively decidable when its associated 1/0-valued function is effectively computable. A formal computation model is fixed to prove machine limitations; the Church–Turing thesis then extends the conclusion to effective procedures.
samples.checks: The isprime cases remain 1 for prime and 0 otherwise. The thesis is a separate premise for the informal effective-procedure claim, not a machine impossibility proof by itself.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: Turing machines can be systematically listed and numbered, whereas all functions from natural numbers to natural numbers, even binary-valued ones, form a nonenumerable set. Therefore the Turing-computable functions constitute only a denumerable set and some functions are not Turing-computable.
samples.checks: !!{nonenumerable} and !!{denumerable} retain their source tokens and are glossed with distinct established Marathi cardinality terms.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: No single Turing machine always halts with the right 1/0 answer to whether an encoded machine M halts on n. That example helps show other undecidable problems, specifically validity of an arbitrary first-order formula. The historical decision problem and its independently established Church–Turing theorem name remain distinct from the Church–Turing thesis.
samples.checks: Both quantification over descriptions and inputs and the always-halts requirement remain explicit. First-order validity is not replaced by truth in one structure; the source's theorem label is preserved.

source_observations: The English source has a grammatical omission in 'cannot effectively decided'; Marathi supplies the intended grammatical form without changing the claim.
The source calls the independent unsolvability result the Church–Turing Theorem. This is preserved as a named theorem and not conflated with the earlier thesis.
limitations: No independent human or native-speaker review has been performed.
The chapter's remaining imported sections have not yet been translated or built into a reader.
